utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. This is Wednesday, July 1st, 2009, and I welcome everyone here, notably Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. I also welcome the counsels from the Defence, notably Mr. Khan, who is always with us, who seems to be in all courtrooms, morning and afternoon. I also welcome Mr. Stringer and the people helping him, and all people helping us also. I believe that Ms. Alaburic has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to Your Honours and everybody else in the courtroom. I wanted to respond to your offer of yesterday that the additional time that I need for -- or additional time for General Praljak's cross-examination I use the time that has been accorded to the Petkovic Defence. I'd like to thank you once again for giving us this possibility, and I'm sure that this was made in the best of intentions, but I cannot accept that proposal for the following reasons, and they are reasons of principle: The Defence of General Petkovic asked for additional time for examining the expert witness, that is to say the accused Bruno Stojic, in keeping with the guidelines issued, timely guidelines, and with the corresponding explanations. Now, our request for a total of four hours for the cross-examination of this important witness was not accepted, but the Honourable Trial Chamber gave us the right to cross-examine for a time of one and a half hours. The Defence of General Petkovic, considering it to be standard practice whereby the Defence has the right freely to distribute the time it has been allotted for presenting its defence case sent to the Honourable Trial Chamber on the 15th of December, 2008, a notice informing them that they will use their own two and a half hours. Approximately one month later, that is to say on the 12th of January, 2009, the Trial Chamber, proprio motu, as regards the notice by General Petkovic, treated it as being an additional request for additional time and refused that request. The Defence of General Petkovic tabled a new request for the reconsideration of the first decision and ruling and -- to appeal against such a decision, but that request was rejected. Therefore, the Defence of General Petkovic was not allowed, to the detriment of its own time, to use its own time to use the Stojic Defence witness Mr. Dvor Marijan during the time that it deemed necessary, that the Petkovic Defence thought was necessary. We considered that thereby the rule had been established whereby the Defence cannot distribute its own time in such a way as to extend the cross-examination of a defence witness from another Defence team. With every respect for the ruling and position taken by the Trial Chamber, the Petkovic Defence, during the defence of Mr. Stojic, and never again repeated the same request. The proposal made yesterday, it seems to me that the Trial Chamber changed its position on this topic. Now, to avoid any misunderstanding with respect to your question, the Petkovic Defence at this point in time is making an oral motion and requesting that the Honourable Trial Chamber define its position with respect to the right of using its own time by a Defence team in order to prolong the cross-examination of the witness of another Defence team -- or, rather, to define whether it is going to change the position it took during the Stojic Defence case. The Petkovic Defence considers that by changing the position on this important issue the right of an accused to a fair trial would be violated along the lines of Article 20 of the Statute, and Article 21(1) of the Statute on equal rights and equality of arms for the accused. Of course, it is possible that the Petkovic Defence has erroneously evaluated the possible arguments as to the change in the Trial Chamber's position, and therefore we expect that a decision on this oral motion will be explained in the proper way, and the Petkovic Defence, depending on how the decision is expounded, will see whether it needs to seek legal remedies against that decision or not. If the arguments put forward in the opinion of the Petkovic Defence are not contrary to the Statute and the rules of in Tribunal, then we will not oppose such a decision. However, if we consider that by changing the position on the part of the Trial Chamber one Defence team would be privileged to the detriment of another, in this case General Praljak's Defence and maybe the Petkovic Defence as well, we will oppose such a change with respect to this important decision. That is all, Your Honours, and thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Trial Chamber will deliberate on this and we'll issue a decision. Let me give the floor to my fellow Judge, but personally, first I have something to say, something that I wrote in a good number of opinions, and would I like to state it again. As far as I'm concerned, the cross-examination in its common law sense, as resulting from the Rules of Procedure, is for the following: It's whenever what the witness is saying is against your own interest. Up until now, I really don't see how Mr. Petkovic's interest can differ from those of Mr. Praljak. You'll have to demonstrate this to me. So far Mr. Praljak has testified for dozens of hours, and I don't see where or when he actually challenged or questioned Mr. Petkovic. First thing. Second thing, this morning I was listening to other trials, like -- because I usually do this to try, you know, and learn, and I was listening to the pre-trial conference of Mr. Karadzic, and I noted that in the time that has been allotted for cross-examination, Judge Bonomy in person said that cross-examination would be allowed 60 per cent of the time. I'm sure you know that here it's a hundred per cent of the time that is allotted. So we were extremely generous. I even believe that we were excessively generous. We should have placed limits on this. The problem is we placed no limits and now we run into problems. Thirdly, we gave you an extra 45 minutes. You know, you only had four hours. We gave you an extra 45 minutes which was taken from the time that would the no be used by Mr. Pusic's Defence. So we were lenient once again. You did not agree with this. The Trial Chamber deliberated on this yesterday and said, Well, if Ms. Alaburic needs time, well, she can just use her credit, the credit that she has. So this was really extremely generous on our part. You still aren't happy with this decision, and you're still coming up with the problem again, talking about major principles, equality of arms, and so forth and so on. Let me tell you, as far as I'm concerned, I can tell you as legal professional that neither in the Statute or in the rules of procedure or anywhere in any national documents do we have this problem, is there anything on the limits of time. It's up to the Judges to decide, always. We have to rationalise our time. We have to save time, and time, you know, is not infinite. Of course not. And we have to take this into account. Of course, if during your cross-examination we note that there are very important questions that require additional time, what do the Judges do most of the time? You saw what we do here, you know, which is something that is -- that is not done in other Trial Chambers. We Judges put questions, you know, and the time that we use to put questions is not taken, deducted from your allotment. So why do you complain? We could just, you know, not say anything, stay silent and let you operate. If you'd rather have it that way, just tell us. But then instead of giving you four hours, maybe we will give you an extra 20 or 30 minutes and we will not put any question to the witness. But you're complaining, and I really don't understand why you keep complaining. You made your oral motion. Fine. You will get a decision to answer this motion. I don't know what my fellow Judges have to say. I'm sure that they all have their own opinion, and my colleague Judge Trechsel wanted the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, first of all of course I agree. We will examine the question and give you an answer. But, I would indeed like to hear with a bit more precision why you consider that the -- a change which would -- if it is a change. I'm not aware that we actually ever really discussed this. I'm not aware that we discussed it. But if we now were to change the practice in that we would allow Defence teams to make use of their time credit to cross-examine witnesses, in what way do you consider that this could impair the fairness of proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to thank Judge Antonetti and Judge Trechsel for their observations. I'd just like to put right something that Judge Antonetti said recorded on page 5, line 3. His Honour Judge Antonetti said that I did not agree with the decision made by the Honourable Trial Chamber whereby the Petkovic Defence would be given an additional 45 minutes from the time remaining with respect to Mr. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and the Pusic Defence. That assertion is not correct. I did not challenge that decision in any way, nor did I require leave to appeal the decision. All I did was yesterday at the beginning of the cross-examination, I said that all the documents had been prepared on the assumption that I had six hours, but if I did not have six hours, then I would skip over some subjects and some areas. That's all I said. So in no way did I bring into question the Trial Chamber's decision. Now, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I'm going to repeat what we wrote in our request for reconsideration of your decision not to allow me to use my own time for questioning an expert witness. I reminded you on that occasion that for the presentation of the Prlic defence the Defence teams were allowed to use their own time in order to extend the time for the cross-examination of individual witnesses, and that is an indubitable fact. Now, believing that practice had been established thereby, I asked the same right when it came to Witness Dvor Marijan. I can give you lengthy explanations as to what organisation of time means to each of the Defence teams and the possibility of discussing certain areas using their own time and additionally examining the witnesses of other Defence teams. Had I had sufficient time at my disposal to cross-examine Dvor Marijan, perhaps I would not today using exactly the same documents broach exactly the same topics with General Praljak as the witness sitting in the chair at this point in time. However, at that time I did not have enough time, and from Your Honours' questions I can understand where the problems lie in understanding the competencies for bringing criminal procedures to bear and responsibilities -- criminal responsibilities for crimes committed, and I consider that I had sufficient time to clarify those matters using the Stojic Defence witnesses who came into this courtroom to discuss precisely those topics. Similarly, I consider that it is completely unacceptable that during the Defence case of Bruno Stojic the rule was used whereby one's own time was not used. And I'd like to remind you that none the Defence teams in this courtroom after your decision with respect to the Praljak Defence request for additional time with respect to Dvor Marijan posed a similar request, because as far as we were concerned there was no dilemma as to that being the position taken by the Honourable Trial Chamber. Now, theoretically what can happen is this, for example, the Stojic Defence, for example, has at its disposal some ten hours, I believe, which it did not use for its own examination. Now, if you change your position with respect to the right of using your own Defence, and I'm only putting this as a hypothesis, as a hypothetical, the Stojic Defence can then be brought in to a situation of being privileged whereby at the detriment of their own time, using up their own time in questioning General Praljak or General Petkovic without having to in keeping with the guidelines table a request for additional time with the Trial Chamber and explain the reasons for that, for that request. Therefore, according to the guidelines we all have the right to ask for additional time. That is indubitable. But we would like to convince the Trial Chamber that our reasons are valid ones, and if we succeed in doing that then there is no doubt that we will be allotted time, but if we change the practice with respect to using one's own time credit or credit time, then we will enable other Defence teams outside that rule to extend the time they have for the cross-examination of witnesses from other Defence teams. There, Your Honours, is what I wanted to ask you briefly, and if we are going to appeal to the Trial Chamber decision, then we'll be supplying further explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give the floor to Mr. Stringer so he can tell us what his point of view is regarding what you just said to give us grounds for your oral motion, and the Trial Chamber will then deliberate and we'll issue a decision on this next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours and to everyone else. Beyond observing that we are in complete agreement with what the president's just said about the generosity in terms of time that's been granted, I think to all of the Defence teams, and the flexibility that the Trial Chamber has shown at various times in accommodating the various teams in their wishes to get additional time for cross, beyond expressing our agreement with that, we don't have a position to take in respect of the application by counsel. We don't support it, nor do we oppose it. We think since it goes to cross-examination by the Defence, especially of a co-accused, it's -- it's not for the Prosecution to take a position, and so we will accept, obviously, whatever ruling the Trial Chamber makes on that issue for now and also for the remainder of the Defence cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me just one sentence. I think I'm duty-bound to give you my position as regards the magnanimity or generosity regarding the time allotted to each Defence team. If you are giving the example of the accused Karadzic who was granted the right to cross-examine the witnesses to the amount of 60 per cent of the time that the Prosecution gets, I would like to say that the Petkovic Defence had far less time because we had only one-sixth part of the time allotted to the Prosecution. Other Defence teams are other Defence teams. That's not the Defence of Milivoj Petkovic. As regards the right to the cross-examination of witnesses on the part of -- or called by other Defence teams, well, this is immaterial at this point in time, and I don't think that this was a generous rule. I think it was relatively strict, but I definitely do acknowledge the effort of the Trial Chamber to give additional time to the Defence teams for their examination of the witnesses whenever they could show cause for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will issue a decision on this, and Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor to pursue your cross-examination. Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Apologies to counsel for this, but I -- while we're on procedure, if I could just make one remark or comment for the Trial Chamber. Today we received -- I don't know whether the Trial Chamber has seen it yet or not, but a letter came in from one of the accused, Dr. Prlic, and he's asking essentially for an opportunity to make further submissions of documents. It's a letter. It's not a motion from the Prlic Defence, and I just wanted to clarify that for the record what the status of the letter is, because I want to make sure that the Prosecution has an opportunity to respond to the letter. Our view is that, without getting into the substance of the issue, my own view, if you will, is I remembered a recent ruling by the Trial Chamber in which it was critical of notices that had been filed by parties, and the Trial Chamber observed that it did not consider notices to be motions under the rules and that it wasn't going to consider itself to be seized of things said or asserted in notices so that it wasn't going to issue any rulings on them, and I think the Prosecution position is that in respect of the letter from the accused, it falls into the same category or it should. It's not a motion, and our suggestion would be that if the Prlic Defence wants to make this application by motion, it should do so at which time then the Prosecution would file its response. Otherwise, I'm not sure how we would be expected to respond to a letter that's come directly to the Trial Chamber from an accused, and so we're seeking the Trial Chamber's guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. -- could you please give us some information on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to the Chamber and everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Karnavas, yesterday, after receiving your decision manage to have it translated, and he took the translated decision to Mr. -- Dr. Jadranko Prlic in the detention unit. They discussed the decision, but as of yesterday, no decision was taken on their part regarding this decision of yours. This morning Mr. -- Dr. Prlic spoke to Mr. Karnavas twice and notified him of his wish to send a letter to the Honourable Trial Chamber. Well, you've seen the contents thereof. Now, what status the Trial Chamber will accord to this letter, it's entirely at the discretion of the Chamber. If you want any additional information or if you would like to have a hearing about the status of this letter or to discuss it in any form, I propose that we take 15 minutes of our time at the end of our hearing so that we don't hinder Ms. Alaburic's cross-examination, and Mr. Karnavas will be here to provide any additional arguments that you might require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomanovic, very well. Yesterday the Trial Chamber received the B/C/S version. We were awaiting the translation. We obtained early in the afternoon, and obviously it seems that the accused Prlic is directly calling directly upon the Trial Judges with this letter. It's extremely polite. We have nothing to say about this letter. There is a copy of this letter to the Prosecution as well as to the counsels -- to all counsels of Defence, and he is raising this problem in his letter, but of course he also says that it is a very unusual way to proceed, to write a letter. The Trial Chamber will thus deliberate on the legal status that is to be granted to this letter, whether it will fall within the category of the famous notices that Mr. Stringer told us about. If that's the case, then the Trial Chamber will say that the Trial Chamber only authorises motions filed by the counsels, and because of that the Trial Chamber will not look into this letter, or the Trial Chamber may decide to have a different position, say that the accused is always entitled to seize his Judges, after all, because there absolutely needs to be some circuit between the accused and their Judges. And if that's the decision we choose and that's the avenue we choose, then we will try to do decide on this. But I'm always trying to find the hidden agendas, you know, behind all these letters. I want to know what the real motivation was for writing this letter. Mr. Prlic should have told his counsel, "I don't agree with the content of the Trial Chamber's decision so please make a certification of appeal." That would have been the traditional way of doing things. If he'd rather use another avenue, that might mean something. Maybe there's something wrong, something I don't know about. You know, Mr. -- I already told you, Ms. Tomanovic, the fact that Mr. Prlic does not want to attend the trial means that something is wrong. He might feel that he hasn't been heard correctly, that he is not being listened to, that he has not been understood correctly, which might explain why he no longer wants to attend the trial, thinking that maybe this is just a mock trial. Maybe that's what he thinks. I'm -- I already told Mr. Karnavas all this, because I wanted Mr. Karnavas to try and convince Mr. Prlic come back in the trial. If he had been here, you know, he might have been very useful during the examination of Mr. Praljak either directly or through his counsels. It could have been very useful if Mr. Prlic had been there. It's always better to be there, anyway. He does say that he is following the trial. I hope he is, but I think he would be in a better situation to follow the trial if he were attending it, but you all know that this has to do with the fact that the Trial Chamber did not admit the voluminous work that he did when he drafted a huge document. You know, that was probably very useful to his defence, but you know that for procedural reasons we could not admit this document. It was impossible to admit it. In its decision the Trial Chamber clearly told and showed you that the document could very well be tendered at one point in time, during Mr. Praljak's examination. He could stand up, he could have stood up and said, "I made a study. I would like to admit -- I would like to tender this document that I wrote because it might either confirm or go against what Mr. Praljak is saying." It could have been a procedure that could have been used, and the Trial Chamber thus would have been placed in other legal situation. I must say that in the 30 years of my career it's the first time that I have an accused that does not -- that refuses to attend his own trial. And coming from Mr. Prlic, I must say that I'm quite flabbergasted, especially given the very high responsibilities that he had at the time. So there is a problem some place, and maybe this matter is just a fallout of this problem. We'll take all this into account. We'll look at the human situation, the psychological situation, and the legal situation to try and find a good solution that will satisfy the interests of justice, the interest of your client and the interest of the Prosecution also. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to say the following, that I do agree, of course, with our President, what he has been saying. Just for the record, I would like only to -- to read out the quote, two parts of the letter which I believe are important. Again, let me say that of course the Chamber will deliberate on this issue and will make its own decision. So I believe that in the original letter, Mr. Prlic made two important points, and I quote the first part of it when he said: "I would like to take this opportunity to ask the members of the Trial Chamber simply to grant leave to my Defence to file another motion to introduce new evidence in accordance with the rules established by this Chamber. Of course, no new documents would be introduced. No new documents would be introduced. It is my opinion that this would not constitute a precedent." And now the second point which I believe that is important to summarise and to -- and to quote, it is the following, that: "I would like to take this opportunity to ask the members of the Trial Chamber simply to grant leave to my Defence to file another motion to introduce new evidence," but afterwards, actually the letter continues: "That I do not think that the appeals procedure, which as I understand my Defence wishes to start, is necessary if my request is granted. I understand that it is outside the regular procedure. However, it has a very clear and decent intention, to offer all the parties in the proceedings the relevant documents to make a just ruling." So I quoted these parts in order to shed light on the thinking of Mr. Prlic, but again, as we agree in this Trial Chamber, we are going to discuss this matter further and to -- to reach a decision on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I could add also the last paragraph of this letter, Mr. Prlic wishes the Trial Chamber Judges all the best in their -- in the procedure. So Mr. Prlic is also fully aware that this trial must be held in the best conditions possible, and he would like to contribute to this, and this is good news. Ms. Tomanovic, you might tell him this. It would be even better if he came back, you know, to attend his trial. That way he could give us his point of view. He could actually tell us why the decision of the Trial Chamber jeopardised something as far as he's concerned. I never told any accused not to speak out. So he can come back. He should come back. He should tell us everything, you know, that he has against us and then we could continue with this trial, because it's not good for him to be far from his trial. Obviously, Mr. Prlic must be in despair, you know, and must feel very poorly about being placed in this situation. I believe that everyone now must chip in. He must understand that we do have a Rule of Procedure and Evidence. Contrary to what some people think, it's a very good regulation that really helps -- that allows us to do many things. It's a mixture between civil and common law. As far as civil law, a lot of things are allowed. Of course, some items have been locked by -- in practice by a number of Trial Chambers but it's only because one Trial Chamber will not allow one thing that another Chamber must absolutely abide by that. This is a very versatile Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Judges can ask questions, for example, this is allowed in the regulation -- in the Rules of Procedure. And in the Rule of Procedure an accused can also complain and say why he's not interested with this or that. So Mr. Prlic's interest is to come back in the courtroom to tell us what's wrong. If it's a problem with time, the Trial Chamber has already answered. The Appeals Chamber confirmed its -- the decision, but we can ask the Appeals Chamber once again, you know. It's -- not attending your trial is not a good thing. We were very surprised, you know, the day he left the courtroom we were in confronted with a fait accompli. We didn't expect this at all. No one expected this; whereas as if he had opened his heart before, you know, and told us about what was wrong, you know, we would have found a solution. We will study this letter and we will issue a decision on this after having deliberated on the question. Mr. Stringer, you want to take the more again?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President, just to clarify. If I understand correctly, the Trial Chamber is going to deliberate and issue a decision, and the decision is going to be about what status to give this so that the Prosecution knows in what we way can file our response, because we obviously want to be able to respond in some fashion to the requests that are being made in this document, so I just wanted to clarify that that's the decision that's going to be coming down as opposed to a decision on the merits of the requests that are being made by Dr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. It's on the statute of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, just very briefly to take some of Ms. Alaburic's time and to thank the Chamber for their comments, since Dr. Jadranko Prlic is regularly reading the transcripts from the trial, he will read everything that you have said, and I will also inform him this evening as I do every evening after the hearing. We discuss at length the developments at the trial, and I believe that Dr. Jadranko Prlic will convey his opinion in a proper way to you. And finally, let me say something that I should have said right at the beginning but I forgot. Mr. Karnavas would like to apologise for not being in court today. He's dealing with some administrative issues that are very important that the Registry has asked him to do, and the deadline is next Monday. But at any rate, if you wish to open any additional discussion on this topic, he can be here within 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will continue with our cross-examination, but my fellow Judge Trechsel has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a very light observation. You have not used Ms. Alaburic's time. It remains intact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I really would not like to get into any conflicts with Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel. I never doubted for a moment that this minor slip of the tongue of my colleague Ms. Tomanovic would be corrected by you and we always count on your interventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Alaburic. Good afternoon to Your Honours and to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we stopped at the second model. The US army is waging war in the US territory, and I have been thinking, trying to avoid any question which would require you to provide a legal opinion of any sort, so I thought that it would be best to phrase my question in the following way: If you were the commander of the US army and if you were to defend the USA on its own territory, would you consider that public law and order would be something that the police would be taking care of and that the perpetrators of any crimes would be prosecuted by the bodies that are duty-bound to do so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it is actually done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you allow me to use the phrases, the wording that you used in your examination-in-chief, does that mean that you, as the commander, are responsible for what's going on at the front line and that the developments in the rear are something that the organs that have this in their jurisdiction would take care of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if I learn of something, if I come across a crime in the course of the commission and if no one else is aware of it, then I am duty-bound to do that. They do it ex officio, but I am also duty-bound if I learn of something to seek assistance from the organs in whose jurisdiction it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, we will deal with this in some greater detail later, but for the time being let's just draw some conclusions. So if we take these two models, the US army occupying Iraq and the US army defending the US territory on its territory, now if we tried to transpose those two models to Herceg-Bosna, what would you say? Is the HVO operating in accordance with the first model or the second model?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not an occupying army. We did not occupy anything. So we were simply -- we simply had behind us an organisation. Well, it was a weak organisation, but such as it was, it was supposed to do its job as best it could. It did its job but not well enough to prevent all those things, but a lot was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, could you please tell me whether the civilian authorities and the military authorities were in fact in embryonic stages, were getting organised and were trying to deal with the situation as best they could?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were indeed an embryo, and those who don't know how difficult it is to create a society, it takes decades, decades, and I could be talking about that for hours. Legal professionals usually believe that as soon as they issue laws, a state of law with the rule of law and order would ensue but that's not the case. Society is the most complicated form in nature which sometimes takes decades to take off the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let's move on to the next topic. We're still talking about documents in binder number 1, and the third topic is the HVO as an element of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and a Joint Command. General Praljak, a lot of the documents in the binder are already in evidence. I have included them, however, because I wanted to provide the Trial Chamber to have as many documents in one place, because those documents confirm that the HVO was a component of the armed forces. Let's go through the documents together, and let's do it as quickly as we can. The first document is P339, an agreement on friendship and cooperation which was signed on the 21st of July, 1992, by Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic. In bullet point 6, General Praljak, it says as follows: "The armed element of the HVO is an integral part --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I believe it is simply a technical problem but to be sure. You said, I quote: "The first document is P339," but I believe it should be 1339. Isn't it so? 1339.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I called number P399. This is the first document in the third group of documents. This is the fifth topic on my list -- or, rather, in the binder, the fifth topic, and [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "armed forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, we're looking at bullet point 6 where it says and I quote: "The armed element of the HVO is an integral part of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The HVO will have its representatives in a Joint Command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina." General, in your opinion would this be an indisputable proof to show that the HVO was part of the BiH armed forces and that together with the BiH army it was supposed to establish a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I believe that I have spent hours talking about this. This is indeed correct and there is nothing to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to skip all the documents that are already in exhibits in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have already asked this same question to another witness, but the witness did not have your political or -- knowledge or military competencies, and I think that you can answer this question. In the document -- the documents is an international agreement signed by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman. It is an agreement on friendship and cooperation, a fairly traditional agreement according to international law. Looking at the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, and you know that I have already asked you several questions on that matter, I had noticed that international agreements had to be ratified by the Sabor. This specific agreement, was it examined by the Sabor? Was it published by the official journal of the Republic of Croatia, or was it an agreement that stayed as a confidential agreement on the shelf and without the Sabor being -- knowing anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement was publicised. It gained a very high profile in public on account of the fact that this was an agreement that opened or provided prospects. Whether it was ever published in the Official Gazette, I don't know. I've never checked that. It was certainly something that was discussed at a session of the parliament. The parliament has a scope of precisely defined activities which enable it to restrict the foreign policy pursued by the president of the state, such as army deployment, not being allowed to change borders and so on. Whether this type of agreement on friendship and cooperation would fall within the remit of the parliament's work and ratification, I can't tell you at this moment because I don't know. But I know some other things, for example, what the president of the state could not do without the approval of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you will agree with me: If you will tell us all the other things that you know we will never finish. So I think it's better if we remain limited to the question. I have another question for you with regard to this text, for instance. On page 20, line 6 following, this afternoon you have said, and I quote: "Legal professionals usually believe that as soon as they issue laws, a state of law, that the rule of law, order would ensue, but that is not the case." Now, I have no idea wherefrom you take your ideas of what lawyers think, because you definitely are not a lawyer, and I can assure you that this is not what an informed lawyer thinks at all, on the contrary. In this case isn't this an agreement which mainly is paper but which never really came to life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, my experience gained in politics and working with legal professionals speaks to the contrary. I've been listening to people, and I still listen to people in the states that pass democratic laws. Only yesterday talking about the ineffectual nonexistence of democracy. I heard that that was the case in Hungary. A vast number of such people, and I will apologise when I say, with all due respect, that I am familiar with law and even fewer people are familiar with sociology and everybody speaks about society. Please don't keep on telling me I'm not a lawyer. None of you are a professor of sociology. None of you have read books. And they still talk -- in other words, my experience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I asked a question, yes. How much of this paper was actually transferred into reality and did not remain paper? A declaration of nice intents which, however, I would say history shows, was not really serious and not implemented.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is as follows: On the Croatian part we honoured everything. Croatia offered and implemented a -- bullet point 4 where it says that they will help in the area of jurisdiction and judiciary. Further on, diplomatic relations were established on the Croatian part. Then bullet point 10, the ministry did meet the ministry of finance; for example, through that ministry Croatia assisted various ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina with performing their job and travelling, for example. Let's go on. Pursuant to this agreement, Croatia received the refugees, raised humanitarian and financial aid. Croatia also helped with every matter concerning sports and athletic competitions and sent delegations and teams of Bosnia-Herzegovina to some large competitions such as the Olympic Games. Croatia consistently advocated matters mentioned under bullet point 1 which is was full equality of the three constituent peoples, and the establishment of constituent units. Croatia provided help with the delivery of electrical -- Your Honour, you've asked me a question, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, and you are well aware of the fact that it related to bullet point 6, and you're talking about all sort of different things. Did that join --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement never took off the ground, but bullet point 6 did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear certainly about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is a huge mistake in the transcript. I don't know how this was translated into English. General Praljak actually said, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, you said that this agreement has never taken off the ground, and this is not what General Praljak is saying, so it is not a dead letter on paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard Judge Trechsel saying this is another dead letter on paper, and I am disputing that, and I'm saying that as far as Croatia is concerned, this agreement was honoured. It was not honoured in terms of bullet point 6 as a result of total resistance on the part of Mr. Izetbegovic and his generals. As far as Croatia is concerned, it was honoured -- honoured in all of its elements, and it would have been honoured even in bullet point 6, because we were trying for almost two years to implement that as well, and there are other documents speaking to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, point 6 you have two paragraphs. Now, you have in mind the first paragraph which is on the way the army is composed and the HVO, and it was necessary to have your point of view. But there's also the second paragraph which, according to me, may be even more important, because we're here talking about the joint criminal enterprise. In the second paragraph it is said explicitly something about the constitutional problems linked to the defence matters in Croatia. Izetbegovic signed and seems that by signing this paragraph he recognises the legality of the Croatian Defence Council, because there's an explicit reference to the effect that it has to be compatible with the Constitution of the RBiH. In your recollection was there at the time at the level of Croatia, I'm not talking here about Bosnia and Herzegovina, any thoughts on the legal and constitutional aspects of this questions. And actually the conclusions we can see them in this second paragraph. And somebody could actually draw the conclusion the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic does not put into question the legality of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Mr. Izetbegovic never questioned the legality of the Croatian Defence Council. All laws that were adopted by the HVO and the HZ HB were expressly worded in the following way: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HZ HB, until a political internal solution was found. All the laws were interim laws, and they were all in compliance with the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. More or less all the laws were adopted from the former Yugoslavia. The few lawyers that were down there of course could not produce hundreds upon hundreds of new laws in such a short period of time. A vast number of laws and regulations -- the regulations were adopted by the Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia, and HZ adopted their respective laws from the federal republican laws. And if you will remember Mr. Jaganjac's report where I say, "Okay, if the Washington Agreement was indeed signed, then the HZ HB no longer exist." HZ HB was not for its own purpose. It was in February 1993. There was nothing in dispute on the Croatian side, and he conveys that as a message as Alija Izetbegovic's advisor to his boss, and he says there's nothing in dispute here. HZ HB no longer exists as soon as the agreement is signed. We have already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have one last question. And I'm saying that you're testifying here under oath, but you know, this means that I attach great importance to the questions as well as your answers. This is a warning, that I'm giving you even at all times. As far as you remember, in the government of the Republic of Croatia and the different meetings you attended, either at that level or at the level of Herceg-Bosna, where you were either just a private or the commander of the HVO, I would like to know whether you knew about the decision made by the constitutional court which in its decision declared that the Croatian Defence Council was illegal. We saw this decision, and consequently, of course, all decrees made by the Croatian Defence Council were illegal also. Were you aware of this? Did you know about this at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, thank you for the warning. I am testifying here with full concentration. I am very focussed, and I believe that my brain is still working quite decently and properly. I am sharing with you everything I know. I'm providing the best possible answers from the point of view of my analytical and synthetical brain, and I'm providing you with very precise information. The decision arrived from the Supreme Court. However, this was accompanied by a piece of information according to which the decision had been reached in an illegal, unlawful way, that people who reached the decision at the Supreme Court were only Muslims and that according to the information that existed at the time, there had been no quorum. They were not in a position to reach any decisions. They even forged the facts, and they said that a judge was there although he wasn't. So that decision is what I'm saying, according to our view, did not have the validity of a legal document for a simple. The conditions were the same or similar to the conditions that were in place when the Republika Srpska was proclaimed. So the existence of Republika Srpska and the confirmation of the Serbian state, because that's its title in the Dayton Accords, is not a document that brings people to the court for joint criminal enterprise. I'm still thinking logically, and I don't think that you can avoid thinking logically at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General Praljak, let's try and speak more precisely. You mentioned the decision by the Supreme Court, and it was in fact a decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I misspoke. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And let's be specific with regard to another point. The proposal of the decision of the Constitutional Court. Judge Antonetti asked you and said that the Constitutional Court was proclaimed by the HVO to be unconstitutional. We have seen documents here according to which the decision to set up the HZ HB was proclaimed unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But since we're on the subject, Judge Antonetti showed me the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, Judge Antonetti, in part of the Constitution it says the purified text of the Constitution passed by the Presidency and that purified text does not mean that it was just simple corrections, but they changed the Constitution. So they sifted through the text and throughout what they did not want. It was a revised text, actually. And so -- and the Presidency of a state enacts a Constitution. Where does that exist, and it's all jumbled up. It's a jumbled up legal act. I don't think we've seen that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a very broad topic, and I'd like us to go back to the questions we were discussing. Let's conclude. Nobody of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever concluded that the HVO, either the civilian section or the military section, would be unconstitutional or unlawful; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General Praljak, let's try and provide an answer about the international ratification of agreements, a question raised by Judge Antonetti, and he's asked the question several times and I'm going to set aside some of my time to go into that area. And may we have on e-court P19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would still like to ask a question with regard to the previous 00339 document. I think there can be no dispute that this is an agreement between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree to that, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Judge Trechsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if one looks at bullet point 6, it appears that obligations are -- are set up for the HVO. That is to say, this is supposed to bind an entity which is not a party to the agreement, because the HVO is neither identical to Croatia nor identical to the BiH. Now, by what arguments can one say that this agreement binds the HVO? You may say that it's too technical a question and that you prefer not to answer because you're not competent. I would absolutely accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, if you'll just allow me to follow -- with a follow-up question to ask the witness a follow-up question, and let's start out from the introduction to this agreement in which it is stated that the agreement was passed after talks between the delegations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. Now, General Praljak, in the delegation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there the Croatian component in that tuce [as interpreted, and therefore in that agreement between two states we have the provision which relate to the HVO as well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very happy by the way you have organised and engineered this question, Ms. Alaburic. You have given the answer, actually, in a tortuous way. What you have explained is obvious, and I'm aware of that. It has nothing to do with the fact that here there are obligations for a party which is not a party to this agreement, full stop. The introduction does not speak of the HVO at all, and the HVO is something different from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think there is no answer to this question, and I think we should go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO is Bosnia-Herzegovina, Judge Trechsel. The HVO is Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here you have talks between two statesmen. One is from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other is from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak, we are sitting in this trial for more than three years. This is the first time that I hear someone pretend, and under oath, that the HVO is Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is most definitely not, but you do not understand such matters, so I will not hold it against you. I think we should go on with the question, Ms. Alaburic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. My answer was very precise and no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak, it is enough. You cannot speak as much and as often and on what you want. I have now asked Ms. Alaburic to continue it, and that is what should happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, we're going to look at the transcript of that discussion --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, Ms. Alaburic. I'm not a chair here. I'm not just a chair, and I should kindly like to ask Judge Trechsel when he makes a point, which he can write down in a judgement, I'd like him to bear in mind that I'm a witness for the truth. Not only just for Judge Trechsel or anybody else but for the truth, and when I say that HVO is part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and is Bosnia-Herzegovina, I don't say that those circles coincide, but it means that the HVO was set up to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the expression I used was quite clear and understandable and truthful. If Judge Trechsel does not agree, then in his judgement he can write down and say Praljak lied and I sentence him to 20 years' imprisonment, but I'm a witness for the truth here and of the truth, and I am talking the floor exactly what that answer warrants or send me home and I'll stay in my cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have some ten documents to go through, General Praljak, and they're going to show precisely what you're saying, and that's my objective, to show the Trial Chamber that the HVO is in fact a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that HVO, in fighting on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is defending Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we'll come to that little by little, step-by-step. I'd just like to propose that we digress for a moment and try and provide an answer to Judge Antonetti's question about the verification of international agreements in the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that I'd like to put up on e-court document P19, which is the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia from 1990, and let us look at Article 133 of that Constitution, and that is the last page of the Croatian text and the penultimate page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Article 133 is the one I'd like us to look at, and we can read it all together. "In which cases international agreements signed by the responsible individuals on behalf of the Republic of Croatia must be verified in parliament and by parliament." We have a situation, first of all, when that international agreement which entails the passage or amendment of laws; secondly, when, an international agreement of a military or political nature or another international agreement financially binds the Republic of Croatia; and third, international organisations by which international organisations or alliances are granted powers, powers derived from the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you say what you're quoting from, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm quoting from the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, which is document -- the document that we can see on our screens, on e-court. We have it in our binders, but this is an attempt to respond to the question raised by Judge Antonetti, and it -- we are in fact dealing with Article 133 and not 33 as the record says, but we have Article 133 up on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General Praljak I'm in the going to ask you anything about that because it speaks for itself, it's quite obvious, and I hope that Judge Antonetti has now received an answer to the question that he was rightly interested in. Let's move on to other documents which had to do with the HVO as a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the next document for us to look at is the decree about the armed forces, the decree law on the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina where we can see that the HVO is a component part. We're going to mix -- skip that document because it already has exhibit status and move on to the next one which is 4D410. 4D410. 4-1-0.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Judge Trechsel's microphone please be switched off, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 4D1524. 4D1524. And this is a piece of information from the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces, Sefer Halilovic, in which at the end of point 1 he says: "The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, within whose composition are the armed formations of the HVO."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that document, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's the third document in order, but it's come up on our screens on e-court, so you can take a look at it there. At the end of para 1, Sefer Halilovic says -- he talks about the armed formations of the HVO being a part. Now, General Praljak, to the best of your knowledge, Sefer Halilovic in his documents, did he treat the HVO in the same way as a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina as we have already seen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever it is to his advantage. When it was to his disadvantage, then he failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. My colleague says it was not transcribed, and my question was whether Sefer Halilovic in his documents also described the HVO as a component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the answer has been correctly recorded, so we can move on. Now, the next document, General Praljak, is 4D1523, and that is a document from the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff. Take a look at the beginning of the second paragraph where it says that in Zenica, in addition to the BH Army units, and then in brackets it says what the BH Army comprises of, and then it goes on to say that there is also the HVO. Now, General Praljak, to the best of your knowledge was the HVO in the Zenica area active as a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, the next document is an exhibit. So we'll skip that, but I'll give the number of the document so it's recorded. It is 1D2077. And the next document, which is also an exhibit, is document 1D2432. Now, General Praljak, we'll stay with that document for a moment because it's one that is signed by Alija Izetbegovic, and that is why it is of special importance. Let us look at point 1 of this order where he says: "The armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina (the BH Army and the HVO) ..." Tell us, please, General, without a doubt Alija Izetbegovic, at least the point at which he wrote this order, considered that the HVO was a component part of the armed forces of BH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's go on to the next document which is also an exhibit, and it is a joint statement by Izetbegovic and Mate Boban dated the 27th of January, 1993. The number of the document is P1329, and at the end of point 2 it says that a Joint Command will be established. Now, General Praljak, you told us that at that time you were involved in the formation of a Joint Command for the two components of the armed forces of BH. Was that how things stood? Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, even before and after that. It went on for a year. There were great efforts made in the course of a year, at least on the Croatian side, to establish a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document. It is 4D19, which is an order issued by General -- well, he was a brigadier at the time it, so I apologise, by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, and it refers to the implementation of a joint statement made by Boban and Izetbegovic, which we looked at earlier on, and in point 3, General Praljak, here it says that: "At the level of the operation zones contact will be made with the corresponding army commands in order to set up joint commands." Now, my question to you is this, General Praljak: Is it true and correct that these joint commands were supposed to be established at the level of the operation zones and then united at the level of the Main Staff -- or, rather, the General Staff of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The document number has been recorded, so we can move on to the next document, which is P1341. And it is an order, once again from Milivoj Petkovic. It is the 28th of January, 1993, and once again based on the joint order by Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic that we saw earlier on, and what is being established here is a coordinating body for the 4th Corps area -- or, rather, for South-east Herzegovina as far as the HVO is concerned, and an order, and let's look at it together in the lower left-hand corner, the order is being sent to the operative zone of the HVO and the 4th Corps of the BH Army. Tell us, General Praljak, to the best of your knowledge at the end of January 1993, in conformity with all these orders and all the previous activities, attempts were really made at establishing a Joint Command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and not only in this operative zone but in all the operative zones where the HVO was in contact with the BH Army, and the parity was a 3:3 ratio, three Muslims, three Croats. And the coordinating body selected people for appointment, and two of these, one Croat and one Muslim, were politicians and the our four were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at the next document which is identical to the previous one, but now it is issued by Commander Arif Pasalic on behalf of the BH Army. It's 4D366. We're talking about the same people, the same coordinating body. The order is completely identical in its contents as the one signed by General Petkovic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have our next document, which is an exhibit. It's P1467. P1467. We will not dwell on that. So let us look at our next document. It's 4D1205. This pertains to the cooperation in the Central Bosnia Operational Zone, or, rather, in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps of the BH Army. General Praljak, this document confirms that in February 1993 the two armies worked together, tried to resolve all the problems. Does that correspond to your knowledge of the events in the field?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you take an active part in the efforts to calm the situation down in Central Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put in a great deal of energy and passion. A huge amount of passion. At least those who know me know what I look like when I'm passionate about something.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So we looked at the documents from early 1993. Now I would like to remind you that some of your statements -- of some of your statements in the examination-in-chief so that we can perhaps confirm some of them once again. You told us that after the Vance-Owen Plan was signed by the representatives of the Bosnian Croats or Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the Herceg-Bosna authorities thought that the war was over, that Boban in fact ordered a demobilisation, and that everybody was convinced, sincerely convinced that joint commands would be set up and that that would be an end for any large-scale conflicts between the BH Army and the HVO. Did I understand correctly what you said in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correctly. This plan was signed by Alija Izetbegovic too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In its entirety?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its entirety as far as the Croats were concerned. So -- well, as regards the territory, the military, the constitutional principles, so the essential elements were signed, and there was this sincere conviction, first of all, that this marked the end to the conflicts, that the Joint Command would be set up, and then Mate Boban, acting on the basis of that belief, which was apparently unreasonable, reduced the number of soldiers. Well, you couldn't even pay their salaries, so a lot of them went abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at what is happening a couple of months later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's nearly a quarter to. I think it would be a good idea to take a break. So you will continue after the break. We'll break for 20 minutes, and we'll continue afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to apologise to the interpreters because it appears that at the beginning of our work today I was going too fast, and they told me that in ten years they have not seen anything of that magnitude, so horrible, and I really apologise and I will do my best to mend my ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, let us move on to our next document. That's P2002. It's an agreement entered into -- in Zenica on the 20th of April, 1993, by Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic in the presence of the representatives of the international community, its organisations. Now, General Praljak, at this point in time I'm only interested in paragraph 1, which states that: "The BH Army and the HVO are legitimate military forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and shall be accorded equal treatment." Now, my question to you, Mr. Praljak -- or General Praljak, I assume that you were aware that this document was signed on the 20th of April in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And to your knowledge is it a fact that in other documents, not only this agreement adopted at that time in April 1993, the treatment of the two armies in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the same, they were treated equally, at least in documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Our next document is an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this document -- now, I don't know if General Petkovic will testify, but if he does, I will ask him a question. General Morillon, did you meet him at one point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- or, rather, yes. On one occasion in Medjugorje, but we didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This French general received a military education in French military schools, and he must make a distinction between nonprofessional army, paramilitary groups, and a traditional army. In this specific document, he chairs a meeting. A meeting is chaired by himself and Mr. Thebault. He says that the HVO is a legitimate army of -- of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could he be mistaken? You met him once. Is he someone that cannot understand what the army is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's impossible based on what I knew about him and from his speeches and public addresses. Well, to my mind, he was one of the most honourable generals of the international community, and he was extremely well-informed and the most objective, the most impartial, to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, please tell us, the fact that you did not meet with General Morillon, apart from this one occasion that you mentioned, is that a consequence of the fact that General Petkovic was in charge of contacts with the international community and the participation in those talks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. General Petkovic was the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, and he participated in the talks. I did not have any functions at the time. When I took that post I appointed him to this duty, since he had been conducting these negotiations, to carry on negotiating on behalf of the HVO. He was authorised to participate and to run the talks as he saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll see documents to that effect. Now let us look at document P2078, 2078. The document is an exhibit. It's a joint statement by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Mate Boban, witnessed by Franjo Tudjman. The date is the 25th of April, 1993. We have seen this statement many times in this courtroom. Let us look at the end of paragraph 3 where it says that the BH Army and the HVO shall promptly start implementing the provisions of the agreement about the BH Army and the HVO being equally legitimate formations and that they shall establish a Joint Command. Please, this is a yet another piece of evidence indicating that the HVO was undoubtedly a legitimate component part of the BH Army armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Perhaps we'll find -- or we will have to tender thousands of such documents. Not thousands just a dozen or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to our next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, you promised to us that you will do your best, not to repeat what you have been doing as far as the problems with the translation is concerned, but now you again and also Mr. Praljak are interrupting each other. Thank you. Overlapping each other, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was not aware of it. I will really do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, General, let us move on to the next document, P2091, 2091. It's the Appendix 1 to the agreement or, rather, statement that we have just seen, which was signed on the same day, the 25th of April, 1993, by Alija Izetbegovic and Sefer Halilovic on the Muslim side and Mate Boban and Milivoj Petkovic on the Croatian side. In paragraph 1 we again see the same statement: "The BH Army and the HVO shall keep their separate identities and organisation of the command." And then in paragraph 2 it is stipulated that they shall form the Joint Command. General Praljak, were you aware of this military appendix to the agreement that was signed in Zagreb on the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at our next document, which is 4D1611. 4D1611. It's an order by Alija Izetbegovic, dated the 16th of June, 1993, where he says: "Immediate cessation of all hostilities between the units of the BH Army and the HVO units is hereby ordered." And in paragraph 2: "Persons responsible for the implementation of this order shall be Rasim Delic and Milivoj Petkovic." Now, General, have you ever seen this order before or is this the first time that you see it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it before, but here I have to add something that is quite unusual. At that time, the BH Army had already attacked Travnik, and this order runs parallel to the 25.000 refugees, Croat refugees, who had had to flee from Travnik, and that's really mind boggling. And that action was ongoing, the action launched by the BH Army in Travnik. So 25.000 refugees are already thundering down the roads and up the mountains, and these orders are issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, we will get to Central Bosnia, and we'll see what was going on at the time, but for the time being, for our topic now, what is important is that Alija Izetbegovic is issuing an order affecting also the HVO units, and he designates the commander, Milivoj Petkovic, as the person responsible for its implementation. That's it. So did you know at the time that Alija Izetbegovic was issuing orders that also pertained to the Croatian component in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Our next document is 4D1586. It's a decision signed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. The date is the 20th of July, 1993. It's a decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in paragraph 1 the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina calls upon the units of the BH Army and the units of the Croatian Defence Council to immediately cease the conflicts, the hostilities. General Praljak, were you aware of the fact that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time issued and made such decisions which affected the Croatian component of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but just very briefly, this followed after Bugojno, after Konjic, after Fojnica, after Kakanj, and after the attack in Mostar. That's what's really mind boggling here. I know what you're driving at, but all those locations that I've just listed were already captured by the BH Army and the population had already been expelled from those places.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We will show all that to Their Honours later. Let us look at our next document. I'll just mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still on this document, as on the others, you have seen that third paragraph. The UNPROFOR also has to play a role, and the Red Cross, in the realisation of the present decision. So there are several hypotheses. There is a criminal judge, and he has to speculate on the basis of different hypotheses in order to find out the truth, and he doesn't -- he has to check all the hypotheses. When we look at this document, the first hypothesis that comes to mind is that Mr. Izetbegovic is joking. He, with his army, started a large-scale operation, the HVO, and he takes this type of decision in order to appear as the pacifist of the conflict. This is one hypothesis. Second hypothesis: What he says in the document is true, that is, there isn't a single conflict but several conflicts. You can see there's the plural. So if there is the plural here, and I attach importance to semantics, if there is the plural it means that there are sporadic conflicts here and there, and maybe as a political leader he himself does not control the territory on a political and military point of view, and maybe he is trying to follow his generals and maybe other units which have hidden agendas. And he's trying to calm the situation down, in particular, in the eyes of the international community. So this was -- that was the second hypothesis. So there could be other hypotheses, but these are the two main ones. Now, what would be your hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one, well, that's not something that I would lean towards, but Mr. Alija Izetbegovic appointed Mr. Cibo in contravention of the electoral results to run the municipalities of Konjic, Rama, and Jablanica. He imposed Cibo because he was his man. And in Bugojno he was the person behind the attacks launched by the BH Army. And now if are talking about an isolated conflict when it wouldn't then be in Kakanj, if Fojnica, in Bugojno, in Mostar, and we would not have a situation with 50 or 60.000 Croats displaced or expelled, whatever you want to call it, but at any rate, there were -- they were no longer in their homes. There was an isolated conflict in Prozor, and we managed to deal with it. These are not isolated conflicts. This is clear-cut and open aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, thank you very much for drawing my attention to the plural of the word "conflicts."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, Praljak, now I would like to put to you the following explanation why -- or hypothesis why the term if plural was used, and then tell me if I'm right or correct me if I'm wrong. In Bosnia-Herzegovina there was no single conflict between the BH Army and the HVO, but it was the case that in some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were different situations so that in parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina the BH Army and the HVO fought the Republika Srpska army together, side by side. There were parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the HVO, in operational terms, was subordinate to the relevant command of the BH Army. We saw Sarajevo and Tuzla, examples of that. In some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were no conflicts at all, none whatsoever, and in some parts of the territory there were conflicts, but does that actually mean that there was a whole series of conflicts in a narrow area, parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina? But we'll go back to the actual objective and what was behind those conflicts. So a series of conflicts in various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina if we look at Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to demystify that. There was no need for the BH Army to do anything against the HVO in Bihac for as long as the HVO continued to fight and defend Bihac and die there. There were few Croats there. They were not a problem, because there was a predominant Muslim majority. The same goes for Tuzla and for Sarajevo, which has 97 Muslims living there. There were conflicts where the BH Army had supremacy and a sufficient number of Croats had to be expelled so that they could get the territory. That's Travnik, Zenica, Kakanj, Konjic, and that's where the conflicts were. They needed the territory for the refugees and for a possible set-up of their future state for the Muslims. They needed to create space for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. General Praljak, based on the transcripts of the sessions of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we will see how they planned to spread territories under the control of the BH Army, but let's round this topic off first. The document number is P1234, and in that document, in bullet point 6, there is a reference to the military agreement of the two components of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The next document is 4D1299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
